## Why the First 24 Hours Matter


Speed changes outcomes with lost pets. In the early hours after going missing, dogs often enter a panic phase where adrenaline takes over. Cats tend to go the opposite direction, freezing and hiding close to where they escaped. Either way, the trail is warmest right now.


Even in that panicked state, most dogs don't make it far before exhaustion or instinct kicks in. Research consistently shows that the majority stay within 1 to 2 miles of home during those first 24 hours. The ASPCA found that[85 percent of lost dogs and cats](https://www.aspca.org/about-us/press-releases/how-many-pets-are-lost-how-many-find-their-way-home-aspca-survey-has-answers) were eventually recovered, and the pet parents who found them fastest were the ones who searched the immediate neighborhood and spread the word right away.


## Step 1: Search Your Home and Property First


Before anything else, do a thorough sweep of every room, closet, and corner of your home. Pets, especially cats, are world-class hiders when they're scared. They squeeze into spots you'd never think to check.


-


**Inside:** look under beds, behind appliances, inside dryers and cabinets, in open boxes and bags. Call their name in a calm, steady voice. A frightened pet may not respond to panicked calls.


-


**Outside:** check under decks, in the garage, behind bushes, inside sheds, under parked cars. Scared animals often hunker down somewhere familiar before venturing further.


If your pet is not on the property, leave a familiar scent near the door before you head out. A worn shirt, their bed, or a blanket gives them something to find their way back to. Some pets do circle back, especially in those first few hours.


## Step 2: Search the Neighborhood on Foot


Take your search outside immediately. Bring a recent photo on your phone, a treat bag, and your pet's favorite toy or something that makes a familiar sound.


Walk and call their name calmly. Stop and talk to everyone you see. Delivery drivers, mail carriers, and neighbors who walk the same route every day notice things others miss. Leave your number with as many people as possible.


Timing matters here. Pets often hide during the heat of the day and become more active around dawn and dusk. Do your on-foot search in the morning and again at dusk, checking hiding spots such as crawl spaces, drainage areas, and dense shrubs. Between those walks, drive slowly through the neighborhood with the windows down. Keep your search within that 1- to 2-mile radius for now.


## Step 3: File a Lost Pet Report Everywhere


This step should run parallel to your physical search from the very first hour. Don't wait.


-


**Contact local shelters in person:** File a missing pet report at every shelter and animal control agency in your area. Visit in person when you can. Intake systems get overwhelmed, and a photo and face-to-face conversation leave a stronger impression than a phone call. Check back every day, because a pet that wasn't there yesterday could arrive today. Some municipalities require you to report a missing pet to animal control within 24 to 48 hours, so don't put this off.


-


**Call nearby veterinary clinics:** If someone finds an injured stray, a vet clinic is often their first stop. Call every clinic in your area, leave your number, and describe your pet. Clinic staff can scan for a microchip if someone brings in a found pet, so make sure they know to look for yours.


-


**File a report online:**[Petco Love Lost](https://petcolove.org/lost/) is a free, searchable national database that uses patented facial recognition technology to match photos of lost pets with photos of found pets reported nationwide, speeding up reunions compared to manual shelter checks alone. You can also post your missing pet on[PawBoost](https://www.pawboost.com/) and[PetFBI](https://petfbi.org/) . Use a clear, recent photo and a thorough description on all three.

## Step 4: Post Flyers and Spread the Word Online


Physical and digital outreach work best together. Start both at the same time.


-


**Flyers first:** Print on bright, high-contrast paper with a large, clear photo of your pet. Include the last known location and your phone number. Post them at nearby intersections, park entrances, vet clinics, and pet supply stores. Leave your home address off the flyer. Your number is all a finder needs.


-


**Social media next:** Post on Facebook, Nextdoor, and Instagram with your pet's photo and last known location. Search for dedicated lost-and-found pet groups in your city or county and post directly to them. Nextdoor tends to see the highest neighborhood engagement for lost-pet posts. Ask friends and family to share so you reach people outside your immediate circle.

**Activate Life360's Pet Finder Network:** This is where Life360 members become your search party. ## Step 5: Contact the Microchip Company and Update Your Records


A microchip gives any vet, shelter worker, or animal control officer an instant way to identify your pet and link them back to you. According to the[American Veterinary Medical Association](https://www.avma.org/resources-tools/pet-owners/petcare/microchips-reunite-pets-families/microchipping-faq) , dogs with microchips were more than twice as likely to be reunited with their families compared to dogs without them. Microchipped cats returned home at dramatically higher rates too.


If your pet is microchipped, call the microchip company immediately. Update your contact information if anything has changed, and ask them to flag your pet as lost in their searchable national database. A microchip only connects a found pet to their family when the registration is current.

## Step 6: Know the Shelter and Stray Hold Rules


If your pet was found injured, most people take them to a vet clinic or animal control first. This is why both your microchip registration and those vet clinic calls matter so much.


When you visit shelters, ask specifically about the stray hold period in your state. Facilities are generally required to hold stray animals for a set number of days before making them available for adoption. Knowing that window tells you how much time you have before the situation changes.


Keep your vet records and vaccination records somewhere easy to find. If your pet arrives at a shelter and you need to prove they're yours, documentation gets you there faster.


## Step 7: Don't Stop After Day One


If your pet isn't home by the end of the first 24 hours, keep going. Visit shelters in person every one to two days rather than just calling. Refresh your social media posts so they stay visible. Expand your flyer radius into the next ring of neighborhoods. Most lost pets are successfully reunited with their families, and some are found weeks or even months after going missing. The pet parents who find them are the ones who stayed consistent.


Once your pet is home, microchip and put a pet tag on them if they don’t have one already. They’re the single most effective things you can do before the next scare.
